title: Can Schools Shift From Hierarchical to Relational Leadership Models
author: Nick Hart
summary: Closing his three-part series, Hart takes the can and should questions in turn. The answer to can is a qualified yes, conditional on ceasing to treat leadership as something granted by role. He is candid about the forces working against the shift: time pressure favouring shortcuts over conversation, workload making collaboration feel like a luxury, line management collapsing into oversight, and accountability systems that reward delivery and compliance rather than patient emergence. The emotional obstacle gets particular attention, since many current leaders were promoted precisely because they could fix things and take control, which makes relinquishing the identity of having the answers genuinely costly. On should, Hart argues hierarchies are designed for control, predictability and efficiency and are therefore at odds with systems where insight often sits closest to the problem. He rejects the idea that complexity is new, claiming instead that our understanding of it has changed. Importantly, he preserves administrative leadership for safeguarding, compliance deadlines, crises and resource allocation, insisting only that it cannot be the default mode. The piece ends with a warning against adopting the language of complexity as a buzzword while leading exactly as before, including the trap of heroically leading a school into a complexity-informed era.
points: The structural obstacles Hart names are concrete and diagnosable: line management reduced to oversight, and accountability systems that reward clarity and compliance over emergence.
His account of why heroic models persist is psychological rather than institutional, since they supply identity, certainty and status to people promoted for being able to fix things.
Hart insists relational leadership does not remove structure but realigns it with reality, which is what stops the argument becoming an attack on hierarchy as such.
A specific list of moments where administrative leadership must take precedence, safeguarding, compliance deadlines, crisis coordination and resource allocation, keeps the argument usable.
The final caution is self-implicating: it is easy to become the leader who 'gets' complexity and heroically leads everyone into it, which simply reinstates the hero paradigm under new vocabulary.
quotes: Can schools shift from hierarchical to relational models of leadership? Yes but only if we stop treating leadership as something that is granted by role and start seeing it as something that emerges through relationships.

Time pressure pulls us toward shortcuts instead of conversations. Workload can make collaboration feel like a luxury instead of a priority. Line management structures can reduce leadership to oversight.

These heroic models are seductive because they offer identity, certainty and status. Many of us in leadership positions now were promoted because we could fix things and could take control. Letting go of the identity of being the one with the answers is emotionally demanding.

Hierarchies are designed for control, predictability and efficiency. They assume that problems are solvable from the top, that expertise flows downwards and that clarity is best achieved through structure.

When we default to hierarchy, we risk constraining adaptive capacity, making it harder for people to contribute meaningfully, share responsibility or respond to changing conditions. We mistake control for coherence and we risk losing both.
Shifting to relational leadership models doesn’t remove structure and hierarchy, it realigns it with reality.
It can be another buzzword absorbed into old hierarchies without changing how we lead. It’s easy to be the one who ‘gets’ complexity and heroically lead a school into a complexity informed era.
